# Control-flow graph
## Definition
A control flow graph is the directed graph of the basic blocks of the function (the nodes of the graph) and the control flow between them (the edges of the graph).

 Typically, a basic block consists of a straight-line sequence of instructions or statements. Only the last instruction or statement in each block can perform control flow, and control flow can only be directed to the first instruction or statement in a block.
In most CFG representations, there are two specially designated blocks: the *entry block*, through which control enters into the function, and the *exit block*, through which all control exits the function (typically by returning). Some representations permit multiple exit blocks, especially if there are different kinds of exit, or permit the exit block to be omitted if it is not reachable (see below).
## Examples
- Block 1 is the entry block. It runs from the start of the function until the end of the expression p != NULL. It ends with the if control flow, either entering block 2 if the condition is true or skipping ahead to block 3 if the condition is false.
- Block 2 is the body of the if statement. It ends by unconditionally falling into block 3.
- Block 3 is the exit block. It runs from the end of the if statement to the implicit return at the end of the function body.

Both instrumentation-based and sampling-based profiling techniques work for all programs and have been significantly optimized in prior work([Ball and Larus, 1996](#bib.bib34); [Frenot and Pereira, 2024](#bib.bib37)). Many ML kernels are well-structured with statically-analyzable loop patterns whose executions are fully determined by input matrix/tensor dimensions. Basic blocks and the three leader rules
A basic block is a maximal consecutive sequence of instructions with one entry and one exit. Control enters at the first instruction. Once the block starts, every instruction runs in order until control leaves at the end.
Find leaders before drawing block boundaries:
- The first instruction is a leader. 
- Every target of a conditional or unconditional jump is a leader. 
- Every instruction immediately following a conditional or unconditional jump is a leader. 
After marking all leaders, a block begins at one leader and ends immediately before the next leader. The final block continues to the end of the listing.

In computer science, a control-flow graph (CFG) is a representation, using graph notation, of all paths that might be traversed through a function during its execution, or control flow. The control-flow graph was conceived by Frances E. Allen,[1][2] who noted that Reese T. Prosser used boolean connectivity matrices for flow analysis before.[3]
The CFG is essential to many compiler optimizations and static-analysis tools.
Definition
[edit]A control flow graph is the directed graph of the basic blocks of the function (the nodes of the graph) and the control flow between them (the edges of the graph).
The exact details vary between representations. Typically, a basic block consists of a straight-line sequence of instructions or statements. Only the last instruction or statement in each block can perform control flow, and control flow can only be directed to the first instruction or statement in a block.
In most CFG representations, there are two specially designated blocks: the entry block, through which control enters into the function, and the exit block, through which all control exits the function (typically by returning).

Abstract

Current basic block profiling techniques obtain the count of executions of each basic block in a program using dynamic instrumentation. These profiling counters create runtime overheads and also require the execution of the program, which, for large input sizes, can take substantial time. We propose symbolic program profiling that generates symbolic formulae for a basic block's count with inputs as the independent variables. Our technique is limited in applicability to a certain class of programs, namely machine learning (ML) kernels. We implement our technique in the LLVM compiler and evaluate it on 78 ML operators from 50 different ML models. These operators are generated by TVM, a machine learning compiler. Our symbolic profiles deliver exactly the same results as dynamic instrumentation for 73 out of 78 kernels with a median speedup of 15093x.

seltz.snippet:
Every feedback control system — a cruise controller, a robot joint servo, a chemical reactor temperature loop — is first drawn as a block diagram: rectangles containing transfer functions, circles that add and subtract signals, and dots where one signal branches to several destinations. The diagram is a faithful picture of the signal paths, but analysis and design need something else entirely: a single closed-loop transfer function relating output to input. Block diagram reduction is the algebra that gets you from the picture to that transfer function — a small set of exact equivalence rules (series, parallel, feedback, and four "moving" rules) applied systematically until only one block remains.

For diagrams with more than two or three interlaced loops, step-by-step reduction becomes tedious and error-prone, and a second tool takes over: the signal-flow graph and Mason's gain formula, which reads the closed-loop transfer function directly off the topology of the diagram in one computation. This article covers both — the reduction rules and why each one is algebraically exact, a disciplined multi-loop strategy, two fully worked numeric examples, the loading-effect limits that decide when a block diagram is even valid, and Mason's formula from definition to application. The transfer function you extract here is the starting point for everything downstream: root-locus pole placement and Bode-plot frequency-domain design both begin from the loop and closed-loop functions this page teaches you to obtain.

seltz.snippet: Consider a compiler compiling a matrix-multiplication kernel. It executes its innermost loop body millions of times. Inside that loop sits an array-base address computation, `A[i][j]`. It recomputes `i * stride + base` on every single iteration. This happens even though the values that feed it barely change. A programmer would never write such wasteful code by hand. Yet it emerges naturally from compiling straightforward array-indexing syntax. It is precisely the kind of redundancy that dominates real running time. Loop bodies execute far more often than any other code in a program. Loops are where programs spend almost all of their time. Profiling studies of real workloads consistently show this pattern. A tiny fraction of static code, the innermost loops, accounts for the overwhelming majority of dynamic instructions executed. This "90/10 rule" (roughly 90% of runtime in 10% of the code) explains something important. It is why compiler writers invest disproportionate engineering effort into loop optimizations. ## Chapter 16: AOT Compilation — LLVM IR, MLIR, and the Multi-Level IR Insight

When you compile C, the compiler reads `.c` files and produces a binary. When you compile Rust, the compiler reads `.rs` files and produces a binary. When you compile Swift, the compiler reads `.swift` files and produces a binary. All three of these compilers do something remarkably similar in the middle: they translate the source language into **LLVM IR**, and then LLVM does the rest (optimization, register allocation, native code generation).

LLVM IR (Intermediate Representation) is the universal compilation target. It was developed at the University of Illinois starting in 2000 (Chris Lattner's PhD work) and matured into the dominant compiler infrastructure of the 2010s. By 2026, almost every serious AOT-compiled language uses LLVM somewhere in its pipeline: Clang (the C/C++ frontend), Rustc (Rust), Swiftc (Swift), Crystal, Pony, Zig (initially; now mixed), and dozens more.

But LLVM IR is no longer the end of the story. **MLIR** (Multi-Level Intermediate Representation), also from Chris Lattner's group (starting at Google in 2017, now part of LLVM), has emerged as the post-LLVM infrastructure for serious compiler work. MLIR is where TensorFlow, JAX, Mojo, CIRCT, and the most advanced 2026 compiler projects live. Understanding MLIR is the difference between "writes compilers for one language" and "writes compilers that participate in the modern ecosystem".

This chapter covers both: LLVM IR as the universal target (read a snippet, understand SSA form, know its role), and MLIR as the multi-level insight (write a small dialect, see why "multi-level" matters). This is Workflow #10: a small MLIR dialect for matrix multiplication. We also touch Marisol Hernández's daily work: writing LLVM passes for her chip company's custom ISA.

ultimate.title: Control-flow graph
ultimate.snippet:
A control flow graph is the directed graph of the basic blocks of the function (the nodes of the graph) and the control flow between them (the edges of the graph).

A loop header (sometimes called the entry point of the loop) is a dominator that is the target of a loop-forming back edge. The loop header dominates all blocks in the loop body.  A block may be a loop header for more than one loop.  A loop may have multiple entry points, in which case it has no "loop header".
Suppose block M is a dominator with several incoming edges, some of them being back edges (so M is a loop header). It is advantageous to several optimization passes to break M up into two blocks M pre and M loop. The contents of M and back edges are moved to M loop, the rest of the edges are moved to point into M pre, and a new edge from M pre to M loop is inserted (so that M pre is the immediate dominator of M loop). In the beginning, M pre would be empty, but passes like loop-invariant code motion could populate it. M pre is called the loop pre-header, and M loop would be the loop header.

In this improved block multiplication, we order both the outermost block loops and the innermost block multiplication loops to follow the \(ikj\)-order. The entire computation involves arithmetic operations (counting additions and multiplications separately), but produces and consumes only data values. As a whole, the computation exhibits admirable reuse of data. In general, however, an entire matrix will not fit in a small local memory. The work must therefore be broken into small chunks of computation, each of which uses a small enough piece of the data. Note that for each iteration of the outer loop (i.e., for a given value of i) operations are done and data is referred to -- no reuse.
Now consider a blocked matrix-multiply algorithm. ... First, note that in this program exactly the same operations are done on the same data; even round-off error is identical. Only the sequence in which independent operations are performed is different from the unblocked program. There is still reuse in the whole program of order n. But if we consider one iteration with fixed i0, j0, and k0, we see that operations are performed (by the three inner loops) and data are referred to.
On the other hand, blocked code is much more difficult to write and to understand than point code. Writing it is a difficult and error-prone job.
